titre: Ubisoft games aren't "required to use generative AI," Assassin's Creed publisher says following reports
chapo: Teams reportedly have to say why they don't need the tools

In the latest chapter of the industry's collective embracing of AI, it was reported that Ubisoft was making the tech mandatory for upcoming projects, to the point teams had to justify why they didn't think it was suitable for their needs. The publisher has since put out a statement countering these claims. "We encourage our teams to explore where AI can be useful and bring value to their work," Ubisoft tells Vertical Slice. "This doesn't mean that projects are required to use generative AI." Earlier this week, Vertical Slice reported that Ubisoft now requires pitches for potential releases to demonstrate how they'd use gen-AI. Any team that objected to this apparently needed to state their case for why these tools weren't suitable for their requirements. "Teams need to determine whether, and how, these technologies make sense for the game they want to make and the experience they want to create for players," Ubisoft's statement concludes. According to the original report, anyone who didn't mention generative AI would automatically get a negative response to their proposal. This was all apparently mentioned in a meeting with senior staff. It should be noted that gen-AI isn't said to be compulsory, but Ubisoft's investment is expected to be considerable. Regardless of the level of AI used within the bowels of the Assassin's Creed and Far Cry maker, it's but one of the many games companies embracing the tech. EA, Activision, Capcom, and Square Enix are among those that have utilized AI to some degree in game creation. In some cases, generative assets were found and called out in released projects, including Call of Duty: Black Ops 7. Stats suggest that around 40% of game devs are using generative AI right now, but over half believe it's a net negative in the medium term. titre: Ubisoft reportedly goes all in on company-wide generative-AI use, and if developers don't want to use it, they have to explain why in detail
chapo: Ubisoft is clearly serious about implementing generative-AI deeply into the game development process. extrait: Ubisoft is clearly serious about implementing generative-AI deeply into the game development process. The French publisher now expects teams pitching new project ideas to be prepared to explain how gen-AI will help with developing the game.Teams who don't want to use gen-AI will need to clearly justify their reasoning to the higher-ups. That's according to a new Vertical Slice report, citing multiple anonymous sources currently working at Ubisoft. Several employees said that pitching a game idea without gen-AI or without explaining why it does not involve the use of the controversial tech will not receive the greenlight. This is especially relevant for smaller games with tight teams who now reportedly must deal with Ubisoft leaders' desire to implement gen-AI if they want to get their pitches reviewed. "We were told that using AI will increase the speed at which pitches can be made by 'small lean agile teams,'" one source said. "We were told that as the goal was to move fast, iterate and discard projects to sift out the good stuff. AI was essential in maintaining a rapid pace." While some said Ubisoft is not openly mandating gen-AI use to staff, others feel "cornered" by gen-AI. One source said Ubisoft views the tech as "unavoidable", and that only a minority of the company's audience reject it. Ubisoft recently gave name to an internal initiative to expand the use of generative-AI and research how its developers can make use of the technology. It's called Motherbrain, and it has its own division within Ubisoft. Over a year ago, Ubisoft embarked on a major restructuring effort that has seen the formation of new subsidiaries, the consolidation of its biggest brands into 'creative houses', the closure of studios and, of course, multiple rounds of layoffs. "Ubisoft is in a top-down nightmare of AI psychosis," one source added, pointing to the already low morale within the company. "Yves [Guillemot] has hitched his wagon to the tech, demanding the rest of the company follow on."
